name: Hansons Marathon Method
coach: Kevin Hanson, Keith Hanson, and Luke Humphrey

citations.source: Luke Humphrey, Keith Hanson, and Kevin Hanson
citations.title: Hansons Marathon Method (2nd Edition)

description: High-frequency (6 days/week) marathon system built on the principle of cumulative fatigue. Long run capped at 16 miles. Three quality sessions per week — Speed, Strength (intervals at MP-10sec), and Tempo (Marathon Pace runs of 6-10 mi). All aerobic running done somewhat tired by design.
signature: Cumulative fatigue with a 16-mile long-run cap and three quality sessions: Speed, Strength, and Tempo (marathon pace)
philosophyNarrative: Hansons reject the philosophy of long, leisurely Sunday long runs followed by easy weeks of recovery. Instead, the system builds 'cumulative fatigue' — you train slightly tired all the time so that the back-half of marathon-day fatigue feels familiar. Three principles drive the system: (1) the long run is capped at 16 miles because anything longer doesn't add fitness proportional to recovery cost; (2) marathon pace is the most race-specific pace and gets disproportionate emphasis (6-10 mile tempo runs at goal pace); (3) frequency matters more than any single big workout — 6 days per week of running, with quality on Tuesday (Speed/Strength), Thursday (Tempo), and Sunday (Long Run). All easy runs are intentionally not 'recovered' — that's the point. Training adaptation comes from accumulated stress, not single hero efforts.

paceZones.purpose: The slowest aerobic running. Used the day after Sunday long runs.
Standard aerobic pace for most runs. Hansons intentionally don't make this 'fully recovered' — cumulative fatigue is the point.

rpeRange.description: Conversational; the bulk of weekly running

paceZones.purpose: Hansons' Tempo IS Marathon Pace. The most race-specific pace, done as 6-10 mile continuous Tempo runs.

rpeRange.description: Comfortably hard; rhythmic; sustainable for full marathon

paceZones.purpose: Marathon pace minus 10 seconds per mile — the 'Strength' pace. Used in interval sessions: 6×1 mi, 4×1.5 mi, 3×2 mi, all at Strength pace.

rpeRange.description: Slightly faster than Tempo — controlled but firm

paceZones.purpose: 5K-10K race pace. Used in shorter intervals (400m-1600m) during the Speed phase. Builds aerobic ceiling and economy.
Pace for the 16-mile long run. Slightly faster than Easy — hits the aerobic threshold without going to MP.

workouts.name: Recovery Run
workouts.shortDescription: Very easy short run, typically Monday post long-run

mainSet.description: Easy short run at recovery pace
mainSet.cue: Truly recovery-paced. The day after Sunday long run is for moving the legs, not training.

workouts.purpose: Active recovery the day after long runs and intervals. Even 'easy' days in Hansons are intentionally not fully recovered — but the day after long run is the exception.
cues: Slower than Easy pace by 1-2 min/mile
Walk breaks are fine if needed
If genuinely depleted, take the day off

workouts.name: Easy Run
workouts.shortDescription: Standard aerobic run — done somewhat tired by design

mainSet.cue: Conversational, but you're not expected to feel fully fresh — that's the cumulative fatigue principle.

workouts.purpose: Bulk of weekly mileage. Builds aerobic base under cumulative fatigue. The accumulated stress IS the training stimulus.
cues: Conversational pace, but legs may feel heavy from Tuesday/Thursday/Sunday — that's expected
Don't try to make easy days truly recovery — that defeats the system
If you can't hit Easy pace, slow further; don't skip

workouts.name: Long Run (capped at 16 mi)
workouts.shortDescription: Sunday long run — Hansons' famous 16-mile cap

mainSet.description: Long steady run at Long pace
mainSet.cue: Cap at 16 miles. The Hansons' principle: longer runs cost more recovery than they add fitness. The cumulative weekly load builds the marathon-specific endurance.

workouts.purpose: Endurance plus race-specific fatigue. The 16-mile cap is foundational to Hansons — anything longer is considered counterproductive given the rest of the weekly load.
cues: Stop at 16 miles even if you feel great — the cumulative weekly load is what matters
Practice race-day fueling
This run will feel hard later in training because of accumulated fatigue from Tuesday and Thursday

workouts.name: Tempo Run (Marathon Pace)
workouts.shortDescription: 6-10 mile continuous run at Marathon Pace — Hansons' signature workout

mainSet.cue: This IS Marathon Pace, not 1-hour race pace. Hold goal race pace for the full duration.

workouts.purpose: Race-specificity at Marathon Pace. Volume builds across the program: 5 mi → 6 mi → 7 mi → 8 mi → 9 mi → 10 mi peak. The single most important workout in the Hansons system.
cues: Goal race pace, not faster — discipline is critical
If MP feels labored, your goal time may be too aggressive — recalibrate
Practice race-day fueling on tempos over 60 min

workouts.name: Strength Intervals (MP-10s)
workouts.shortDescription: Intervals at Strength pace (MP-10 sec/mile) — 6×1mi to 3×2mi

mainSet.cue: Slightly faster than Tempo. Practice running marathon pace under fatigue with brief recoveries.

workouts.purpose: Strength pace (MP-10) is the bridge between aerobic threshold and race-pace work. Builds lactate tolerance specific to marathon demands. Volume progresses: 6×1mi → 4×1.5mi → 3×2mi.
cues: Pace is slightly firmer than Tempo, but still controlled
Brief recovery (~400m jog) keeps you in the right physiological zone
If reps slow significantly, you're going too hard

workouts.name: Speed (Short Intervals)
workouts.shortDescription: Short intervals at 5K-10K pace, weeks 1-7 of the plan

mainSet.cue: 5K-10K pace. Develops aerobic ceiling before the program transitions to MP-specific work.

workouts.purpose: Develops VO2max and economy in the early phase before transitioning to Marathon-Pace specificity. Used in weeks 1-5 of the program; replaced by Strength workouts later.
cues: First rep at the same pace as the last — even pacing
Form and turnover matter — don't grind
If you can't hold pace, end the workout

workouts.name: Strides

mainSet.cue: Smooth and fast — never sprinting. Build to top speed gradually.

workouts.purpose: Maintains stride mechanics and turnover during high-volume training. Tagged onto end of easy runs.
cues: Quick turnover, relaxed shoulders
Skip if very fatigued

workouts.name: Race Simulation Tempo
workouts.shortDescription: 10-mile peak Tempo at Marathon Pace, late in the program

mainSet.cue: Peak Tempo workout. Practice race-day fueling, pacing, and mental engagement.

workouts.purpose: Race-day rehearsal. The longest MP effort in the program — gives confidence and final fitness check before taper.
cues: Treat as a race-day rehearsal: nutrition, gear, pacing
Hit MP from the first mile; no easing in
If MP feels labored, your goal time is too aggressive

phases.name: Base
phases.focus: Build aerobic base, establish 6-day frequency, introduce Speed work. No MP work yet.
phases.athleteNarrative: Welcome to the Base phase. Your job here is to establish the 6-day-per-week running pattern and let your body adapt to running every day. You'll do Speed (short intervals at 5K pace) on Tuesdays — these are NOT marathon-specific yet, but they build the engine. The 16-mile long-run cap is in effect from day one. Trust it. Easy runs may feel harder than expected — that's the cumulative fatigue principle working as designed.

phases.name: Strength
phases.focus: Transition from Speed to Strength intervals (MP-10 pace). Tempo work begins.
phases.athleteNarrative: Strength phase: the program begins to shape itself toward marathon specificity. Tuesday workouts transition from short Speed intervals to longer Strength reps at MP-10 sec/mile pace. Thursday introduces the Tempo run at Marathon Pace — initially short (5-6 mi), building toward 10 mi by mid-program. Sunday long run remains at 16 miles. The full pattern is now in place: Tue Speed/Strength, Thu Tempo, Sun Long.

phases.name: Tempo + Speed (Race-Specific)
phases.focus: Peak Tempo runs (8-10 mi at MP), Strength intervals, race simulation. Mileage at peak.
phases.athleteNarrative: Tempo + Speed is where Hansons distinguishes itself. Thursday Tempo runs build to 10 miles at Marathon Pace — a peak MP workout that gives you racing confidence. Tuesday Strength intervals continue. Mileage is at peak (50-65 mpw for the Beginner plan, 60-80+ for Advanced). The cumulative fatigue is now constant — trust that this is the training, not a problem to fix.

phases.name: Taper
phases.focus: Reduce volume sharply while preserving intensity. Final tune-up Tempo 10-12 days out.
phases.athleteNarrative: Taper. Hansons' taper is shorter than other systems — typically 10-12 days — because cumulative fatigue is the training stimulus and you don't need to fully shed it. Volume drops, but Tuesday Strength reps and Thursday Tempo continue at reduced volume. Trust the system. The work is done.

weeklyPatterns.notes: Base phase. Single quality session (Speed) Tuesday, all easy fill, Sunday long run capped at 16 mi.
Strength phase. Three quality days: Tuesday Strength + Thursday Tempo + Sunday Long. The full Hansons rhythm.
Tempo+Speed peak. Three quality days. Tempo extends to 10 mi at MP. Long run still capped at 16.
5-day variant. Departs slightly from Hansons philosophy (cumulative fatigue benefits from frequency) but keeps all 3 quality sessions. Recommend user run 6 days if possible.
Recovery week — every 4-5 weeks. All sessions reduced. Quality preserved but volume cut.

taper.notes: Hansons' 2-week taper is shorter than other systems — cumulative fatigue is the training stimulus, so you don't need to fully shed it. Tuesday Tempo at MP keeps neuromuscular systems sharp.

strengthRecommendation.philosophy: Hansons recommend supplemental strength work 1-2× per week — running-specific, focused on hip/glute strength and core stability. 20-30 min sessions. Do on easy days; never adjacent to Tuesday/Thursday/Sunday quality sessions.

crossTrainingRecommendation.intensityGuidance: Cross-training is supplemental and optional. Use only on Monday rest day at recovery effort. Hansons emphasize that running frequency IS the program — don't substitute cross-training for run days.

restrictions.rule: Hansons is built for the marathon. The shorter Hansons Half-Marathon Method exists but uses similar principles. Not designed for ultras or sub-half distances.
restrictions.warningMessage: Hansons is optimized for the marathon. For 5K-10K specifically, Daniels' VDOT system is a better fit.

restrictions.rule: Beginners often struggle with the cumulative fatigue principle and the 6-day frequency. Best suited to runners with at least one marathon completed and 30+ mpw base.
restrictions.warningMessage: Hansons assumes cumulative-fatigue training and 6 days/week. For your first marathon, consider Higdon Novice — gentler ramp, fewer days/week.

restrictions.rule: Plan requires 6 days/week running availability. Cumulative fatigue principle breaks down at lower frequencies.
restrictions.warningMessage: Hansons requires 6 days/week running. With fewer days, the cumulative fatigue principle that defines this method doesn't work as designed. Consider Higdon (4-5 days) or Daniels (5 days).

invariants: Long run capped at 16 miles — never exceed this regardless of weekly mileage
Quality sessions: Tuesday (Speed/Strength), Thursday (Tempo), Sunday (Long Run)
Easy days are intentionally not full recovery — cumulative fatigue is the stimulus
Cutback every 4-5 weeks at 80% of peak
If user has fewer than 6 days/week available, warn that cumulative fatigue principle is compromised
